chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Ibn Fadhl, from Thal'abah ibn Maymun, from al-Hasan ibn Harun, the seller of silk fabrics, who said:

I was sitting with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and Mu'alla ibn Khunays asked him: 'Will the Qa'im (the Awaited Imam) proceed in a manner contrary to the conduct of Ali (peace be upon him)?' He said, 'Yes, and that is because Ali (peace be upon him) proceeded with generosity and sufficiency (giving enough to satisfy), because he knew that his Shia would be victorious over their enemies. And indeed, when the Qa'im rises, he will proceed among them with the sword and booty (taking captives and spoils), and that is because he knows that his Shia will never be victorious over their enemies after him.'

key_terms.السَّيْفِ وَالسَّبْيِ: The sword and booty (military conquest with taking captives and spoils)
key_terms.الْقَائِمُ: The Qa'im (the Awaited Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi)
key_terms.الْمَنِّ وَالْكَفِّ: Generosity and sufficiency (giving enough to satisfy without excess)
key_terms.سِيرَة: Conduct, manner of proceeding, or administrative style

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the conduct of Imam Ali and the Qa'im regarding victory and spoils?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the strategic wisdom of Imam Ali (AS) in adopting a policy of generosity ('al-mann wa al-kaff') to consolidate power, contrasting it with the Qa'im's (AS) use of decisive military force ('al-sayf wa al-saby') to establish final authority. Shia scholars interpret this distinction as reflecting the different political contexts: Imam Ali faced internal dissent and needed to win over his base, whereas the Qa'im’s era is characterized by the ultimate triumph of the Shia where such consolidation is no longer necessary. This underscores the dynamic nature of Imamate governance, adapting methods to the specific needs of the community's stability and victory.
